readerTitle: Twelve strengths lost to one promise
caseNote: 가상 사례 (식당 용품 유통업체, 철물점, 제조사 사내 데이터팀) · 반례 형식: 장점을 많이 나열할수록 강해진다는 믿음을 뒤집음
insight: 가치 제안은 우리가 가진 장점의 목록이 아니라, 특정 고객에게 하는 특정 결과에 대한 약속이다. 경쟁사도 기꺼이 똑같이 쓸 수 있는 문장이라면 제안이 아니다.
misconception: 장점을 많이 나열할수록 고객을 설득할 이유도 많아진다. '품질, 서비스, 합리적 가격'이면 충분한 가치 제안이다.

sources.text: Lanning, M. J. & Michaels, E. G. (1988). A Business Is a Value Delivery System. McKinsey Staff Paper.
모든 사례와 문구는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 'value proposition'이라는 용어의 기원을 Lanning & Michaels(1988) McKinsey Staff Paper로 보는 것이 통설입니다. 게시 전 저자명·연도·제목을 다시 확인하세요.
유통업체, 철물점, 데이터팀 사례와 모든 문구는 가상입니다. 수치나 실제 기업 사실은 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Twelve strengths lost to one promise
body: A regional distributor of restaurant supplies printed a glossy brochure listing twelve strengths: wide range, fair prices, friendly reps, reliable delivery, and eight more. Every one was true.
A smaller rival's flyer said one thing: *Order by 10 p.m., on your shelves before you open.*
Within a year, the rival had won several of the distributor's best kitchens.

image.label: A thick brochure next to a one-line flyer
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에 글씨가 빽빽한 두꺼운 브로슈어(체크 표시 12개), 오른쪽에 큰 글씨 한 줄만 있는 얇은 전단지. 주방 조리대 위, 셰프의 손이 전단지 쪽을 집어 듦. 실제 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: One line on the window and the van.
body: You run a hardware store across town from a big-box chain. Most of your profit comes from small building contractors.
You can put one line on your shop window and your delivery van. Which one?

options.text: Quality, service and value: everything for your home
options.feedback: It sounds safe and offends no one. But the big-box chain could print the same words, so it gives a contractor no reason to drive across town.

options.text: Contractors: phone your order by 7 a.m., and it's waiting at the counter when you arrive
options.feedback: It names who it's for and the result they get: no time lost on a job day. You give up appeal to casual shoppers, but gain a reason for your best customers to choose you.
Concrete, and better than A. But it describes what you have, not what the customer gets, and the chain probably stocks more.

cards.title: More claims, fewer reasons.
body: The distributor's twelve strengths were all real. But each was something any rival could say too. Busy chefs read "fair prices, great service" and remembered nothing.
The rival's line answered the question a chef actually had at 11 p.m.: *will the stuff be here when I open?*
The long list didn't add up to twelve reasons. It **buried the one reason** that mattered.

image.label: Twelve small arrows versus one large arrow hitting a target
image.brief: 과녁 하나. 왼쪽에서 작은 화살 12개가 사방으로 흩어져 과녁을 빗나가고, 오른쪽에서 굵은 화살 하나가 정중앙에 꽂힘. 과녁 중앙에 "Open on time" 라벨.

cards.title: The value proposition
body: A **value proposition** is a clear promise: *for this customer*, *this result*, *better than what they'd otherwise use*.

It isn't a slogan or a feature list. It's the reason a specific customer picks you. The term is usually traced to a 1988 McKinsey paper by Michael Lanning and Edward Michaels, who argued a business should be built around the value it promises to deliver.

image.label: Three linked parts: who, result, why you
image.brief: 세 칸이 화살표로 이어진 인포그래픽. "Who it's for" → "The result they get" → "Why you, not the alternative". 각 칸에 간단한 아이콘(사람, 체크, 별).

cards.title: Three quick tests.
body: Read your current pitch and check it against these:
list: **Who:** can you name the customer it's for?
**Result:** does it describe what they get, not what you have?
**Why you:** would a competitor be unhappy to see it, or would they happily print the same words?
cards.callout: "Quality, service and value" fails all three.
cards.softwareNote: Many software home pages promise "the all-in-one platform to boost productivity." Compare: "For finance teams under 20 people: close the month in two days, not ten." The second one names a user, a result, and invites a test.

cards.title: A promise is a cost, not just a sentence.
body: The rival's 10 p.m. promise only works if trucks, staff and stock make it true every night. Break it a few times and the proposition becomes a joke your customers repeat.
Choosing one customer also means others won't feel spoken to. That's the price of being chosen by the right ones.
And writing a proposition doesn't prove it. Only customers' behavior does.

cards.title: Now it's a team inside a company.
body: You lead a five-person data team inside a mid-size manufacturer. Other departments mostly ignore you. You get one slide at the next leadership meeting.

options.text: We provide data, dashboards and analytics across the business
options.feedback: Covers everything, so it promises nothing in particular. Managers can't tell what changes for them if they use you.

options.text: Plant managers: every Monday by 9 a.m., a one-page view of last week's machine downtime
options.feedback: It names who, what result and when. You serve fewer people at first, but they'll feel the difference and ask for more.

options.text: We now have a modern data platform and five skilled analysts
options.feedback: Shows capability, which builds some trust. But it describes what you have, and leaves managers to guess what's in it for them.

cards.title: Promise one customer one result, better than their alternative.
body: A list of strengths tells customers what you have. A value proposition tells a specific customer what they'll get and why you.
**Try it today:** finish this sentence: *For [customer], we [result], unlike [what they use now].* Then ask whether a competitor would happily sign it.
